title: How a Few Speak for Many
question: How can data from a few people tell us about everyone?
hook: Nobody asks every resident, yet statistics still claims to know what a country thinks.
idea: Statistics summarizes the data you collected, and random sampling lets conclusions reasonably carry from the sample to the whole population.

beats.prompt: A city of 500,000 people wants to learn how residents feel about a new park, and cannot ask everyone. How should it pick whom to ask?

choices.label: Ask only people standing at the park gate
choices.feedback: Easy to do, but nothing assures that these people stand for everyone else.

choices.label: Ask only those who volunteer by email
choices.feedback: Volunteers are not a random draw, so their views may not extend to the whole city.

choices.label: Ask the first ten people you meet
choices.feedback: It is quick, but the choice is not random, so nothing assures the results extend to the city.

beats.explain: Random sampling assures that inferences and conclusions can reasonably extend from the sample to the population as a whole.

beats.prompt: Sort each activity into the kind of statistics it belongs to.
items: Computing the mean of a sample
Drawing conclusions from data subject to random variation
Making statements about a population from a sample
beats.explain: Descriptive statistics summarize a sample using indexes such as the mean or standard deviation; inferential statistics draw conclusions from data subject to random variation.

beats.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
beats.explain: Errors are classified as random (noise) or systematic (bias), and a Type I error rejects a true null hypothesis, giving a false positive.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?
steps: We want to learn about everyone in a country.
We cannot collect data from every member.
So we survey a sample chosen at random.
Therefore the results describe only those surveyed and can never reasonably extend to the country.
beats.explain: Random sampling assures that conclusions can reasonably extend from the sample to the population as a whole.
